findings.title: prisma is used but never imported in SalesforceCalendarService
findings.body: The new token-refresh block calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` (line 96) and the file's import list contains no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a compile-time failure (type-check/build breaks) and, if it somehow ran, a runtime ReferenceError. The newly added refresh flow can never work as shipped.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema is broken and strips fields, corrupting stored credentials
findings.body: The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]", so the 'any numeric property is the expiry' and 'allow other properties' intent is not implemented. Worse, z.object() strips unknown keys by default and this helper returns `safeParse(...).data`, so when credential sync is enabled every caller receives only `{access_token}` plus the injected `refresh_token: "refresh_token"` placeholder (line 26). Concrete consequences: ZoomVideoAdapter computes `expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` = NaN and persists it; Google's stored key loses expiry_date/scope/token_type; Salesforce's stored key loses instance_url/signature/token_type (breaking the next getClient call since instance_url becomes undefined); Office365 calendar credentials get their real refresh_token overwritten with the literal string "refresh_token". The schema needs `.passthrough()` and a real expiry field, and the fake refresh_token should not be persisted into the credential.

findings.title: Google token refresh crashes in sync mode: fetch Response has no `.data`
findings.body: When credential sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a `fetch` Response, but the non-sync path returns a gaxios response whose token lives in `.res.data`. The code does `const token = res?.data;` then `token.access_token`, which is a TypeError (reading property of undefined) for every Google Calendar token refresh when sync is on — i.e. any booking/calendar operation after access-token expiry throws. The response from the sync endpoint must be JSON-parsed before use.

findings.title: HubSpot refresh stores garbage credentials in sync mode
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens` in sync mode returns a `fetch` Response, but the code treats it as a HubspotToken: `hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken` is undefined (so `setAccessToken(undefined)` is called) and `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` is undefined, making `expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` = NaN. That NaN expiryDate and the empty token are then persisted to the credential via prisma.update, silently corrupting the stored credential and breaking subsequent HubSpot operations.

findings.title: credentialId passed to refreshOAuthTokens instead of userId
findings.body: The third argument of `refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFn, appSlug, userId)` is documented and used as the Cal.com user id sent to the credential sync endpoint, but the Zoho Bigin adapter passes `credentialId` (the credential row id). When sync is enabled the endpoint receives a credential id as `calcomUserId`, so it will fail to find the user or return another entity's credentials — token refresh for Zoho Bigin cannot work under sync.

findings.title: Zoho CRM refresh throws TypeError in sync mode: fetch Response has no `.data`
findings.body: In sync mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a `fetch` Response, but the code immediately accesses `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error`. A fetch Response has no `.data` property, so this is a TypeError (cannot read properties of undefined) on every Zoho CRM token refresh when credential sync is enabled — the adapter was only adapted for the axios response shape.

findings.title: Zoom stores NaN expiry_date and destroys the stored refresh token in sync mode
findings.body: When sync is enabled, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` validates against the minimum schema and strips the response, so `newTokens.expires_in` is undefined and `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` is NaN, which is persisted to the DB. Additionally `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` writes the literal placeholder string "refresh_token" over the real refresh token. The credential is left with a NaN expiry (so `isTokenValid`'s comparison is always false and the stale access token is reused indefinitely) and is unrecoverable if credential sync is later disabled.

findings.title: Webex refresh always fails in sync mode: full schema validated against sync response
findings.body: Unlike Zoom/Office365, the Webex adapter wraps its refresh in `refreshOAuthTokens` but still validates the response with the full `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse`, which requires scope (exact literal), token_type, and refresh_token — none of which the credential-sync endpoint returns (it only returns access token + expiry). Every Webex token refresh under sync mode will reject with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". It should use `parseRefreshTokenResponse` like the other adapted apps, or the schema needs to differ per mode.

findings.title: Lark refresh incompatible with sync response shape
findings.body: The refresh result is passed to `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, this.log)`, which expects Lark's envelope `{code: 0, data: {access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, refresh_expires_in}}`. The credential-sync endpoint returns a plain `{access_token, expiry}` body with no `code`, so `handleLarkError` will treat it as an error (or `data.data.*` will be undefined), making Lark token refresh fail — or worse, persist credentials with undefined refresh_token/refresh_expires_date — whenever sync is enabled.

findings.title: MS Teams credential key replaced wholesale, dropping refresh_token and email
findings.body: In `refreshAccessToken`, `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: responseBody } })` replaces the entire stored key with the refresh response. In sync mode the response only contains access token + expiry, so the persisted credential loses `refresh_token` and `email`. Even though the parent app is the source of truth while sync is enabled, the local credential is silently destroyed: turning sync off, or any code path that hits the local refresh (e.g. a team credential where userId is null and `refreshOAuthTokens` falls back to the local refresh function) will then fail because the refresh token is gone.

findings.title: Outbound credential sync request carries no authentication
findings.body: The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` — no shared secret, signature, or header of any kind. The endpoint's response contains the user's third-party access token, so unless the self-hoster independently protects that URL, anyone who can reach it and guess/enumerate a user id can retrieve arbitrary users' OAuth access tokens. The webhook flow in the other direction is authenticated with CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET; this direction should send a comparable secret (e.g. the same webhook secret as a header).

findings.title: Webhook handler: no method check and unhandled parse/decrypt errors return 500s
findings.body: The handler never checks `req.method` (a GET with no body will run the logic), and it uses `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` (throws ZodError on malformed input) plus `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` (throws on wrong encryption key or non-JSON plaintext). All of these are unhandled, so invalid requests produce opaque 500 errors instead of 400s. Use `safeParse`, wrap decryption, and gate on POST.

findings.title: Credential sync does not reset the `invalid` flag on update
findings.body: When updating an existing credential the handler only sets `key`. If the credential was previously marked `invalid: true` (e.g. by the invalid_grant handling in Google/Zoom/Webex), pushing fresh valid keys through the webhook will not re-enable it — the app stays broken for that user even though the sync succeeded. The update should also set `invalid: false`.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with plain string inequality
findings.body: `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is not constant-time. For a shared-secret check on an endpoint that can write OAuth credentials, use a timing-safe comparison (crypto.timingSafeEqual) to avoid leaking the secret byte-by-byte to an attacker who can measure response times.

findings.title: Salesforce connection is created with the stale access token after refreshing
findings.body: The new code refreshes the token, persists it, but then constructs `new jsforce.Connection({ ..., accessToken: credentialKey.access_token, ... })` using the OLD (possibly expired) token from the credential snapshot instead of `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`. So the refresh has no effect on the connection actually used, and expired credentials stay broken. Additionally there is no expiry check, so this token refresh + DB write happens on every single `getClient` call (every booking), which is both a performance problem and a rate-limit risk against Salesforce's token endpoint.

findings.title: Success check `response.statusText !== "OK"` is unreliable
findings.body: HTTP status text is not guaranteed to be "OK" (it can be empty, e.g. HTTP/2, or localized by some clients/proxies). Use `response.ok` / `response.status === 200` instead; otherwise valid responses may be rejected as errors and refresh may fail spuriously.

findings.title: No tests for the webhook or the sync-mode refresh paths
findings.body: The PR adds a new externally-callable endpoint that writes OAuth credentials and rewires token refresh for ~10 apps behind an env flag, with zero automated tests (the checklist explicitly says no tests were added). At minimum: webhook auth/validation/404/200 paths, and refresh behavior for each adapted app with sync both enabled and disabled. Given the number of adapters that break in sync mode (Google, HubSpot, Zoho, Webex, Lark, Zoom), tests would have caught most of these regressions before merge.
